title: Post 3: How Has the American Workweek Changed?
text:
In 2000, Americans aged 65 and older who worked during the survey reference week averaged about 30 hours of work. Those aged 16–24 averaged roughly 33. By 2024, their positions had reversed: older workers averaged about 33 hours, younger workers about 31. Older workers had not become the longest-working group, but this reversal complicates a familiar question: Are Americans working more or less? The answer depends on whose working week we examine.
That distinction matters because employment counts measure how many people work, not how much time they contribute. Someone working twenty hours and someone working forty can each count as one employed person, despite different labor inputs and time available for education, caregiving, or other activities. Comparing age groups can reveal changes hidden within national averages. Separating main-job hours from other-job hours adds another question: How did actual weekly working hours change across age groups between 2000 and 2024, and where did those changes occur?

Workers aged 25–64 occupy a relatively stable corridor in Figure 1, generally averaging around 39–42 hours. The youngest and oldest groups sit below that corridor, but move in different directions. Younger workers’ hours fell early in the period, declined further around 2009, and subsequently recovered somewhat. Older workers’ hours generally increased, reaching a higher level around 2021 before retreating. The middle groups also ended below their starting levels, although their declines were interrupted by recoveries. This is a story of divergence and fluctuation, rather than a uniform shortening of the working week.
The analysis uses IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly microdata covering 300 months from January 2000 through December 2024. It retains civilian workers aged 16 and older who actually worked during the reference week, had positive sampling weights, and had valid information for all three hours measures. Monthly averages use the individual weight WTFINL; annual estimates average the twelve monthly estimates equally. These are actual hours worked last week, rather than usual or contracted hours. Consequently, the older group’s increase describes people who were working; it does not establish that older Americans generally worked more or became more likely to hold jobs.

Separating the working week reveals where most of the movement occurred. Figure 2 closely resembles Figure 1: older workers’ main-job hours increased, younger workers’ hours declined, and the middle groups retained their fluctuations. Because the figures share a vertical scale, their levels and movements are directly comparable. The age divergence therefore appears primarily in the main job, directing attention toward changes in principal work arrangements.

Other jobs operate on a much smaller scale. In 2024, their contribution averaged approximately 0.6–0.85 hours per week across age groups, with workers aged 45–54 highest. But “less than an hour” does not describe a typical multiple-job holder’s additional workload. Confirmed single-job holders contribute zeros, spreading additional hours across the entire retained sample. This average reflects both how common multiple jobs are and how many additional hours their holders work.
 
The shares reinforce this interpretation: main jobs consistently account for approximately 98% of total hours. Figure 4’s narrow vertical range makes small changes look pronounced. Meanwhile, younger workers often have relatively high other-job shares without the highest other-job hours, partly because their total hours are lower. These annual shares divide average component hours by average total hours; they are not averages of individual shares. Retained inconsistencies between reported components and totals mean the two shares need not sum exactly to 100%.
The reversal remains descriptive. Older workers’ average could rise because individuals work longer, because shorter-hours workers leave employment, or through both processes. These repeated age-group comparisons do not follow the same individuals over time. Actual reference-week hours can also reflect temporary absences, while annual averaging conceals within-year changes. Complete-case selection, retained top-coded values, and inconsistent records may affect estimates. Without survey-design confidence intervals or significance tests, visible differences cannot establish statistical significance or causation.
The central finding is a reversal between the youngest and oldest working groups, concentrated in main-job hours. Explaining it requires learning who stayed in work, who left, and how their principal jobs changed.

title: Blog 5: Is Living Alone Easier Where More People Do It?
text:
North Dakota and Florida tell two different stories about living alone. In 2024, 14.9 percent of North Dakota residents lived by themselves, compared with 11.0 percent in Florida. Yet among adult solo renters with positive income, 20.9 percent in North Dakota faced annualized gross rent above half their income. In Florida, the figure was 42.3 percent. Living alone was more common in North Dakota, but severe rent burden was roughly twice as common in Florida. Why do the two maps of independent living look so different?
The question matters when deciding whether a place fits your budget. Calculating rent as a percentage of your income is straightforward; understanding that number takes context. Is your housing budget unusually stretched, or do many solo renters nearby face similar pressure? State comparisons offer a broad benchmark, although they cannot tell you whether a particular apartment is overpriced. A high rent-to-income ratio can reflect expensive housing, limited income, or both. To explore that distinction, I used the 2024 American Community Survey through IPUMS USA, examining 135,366 adult one-person households that pay rent across the 50 states, with Washington, D.C., kept separate.
The first answer is that stretched budgets are widespread. Among solo renters with valid positive income, 60.6 percent had annualized gross rent above 30 percent of income, and 33.1 percent were above 50 percent—the severe-burden threshold used here. Figure 1 places those state estimates alongside the national benchmark. Florida and Nevada were both near 42 percent, while South Dakota was at 18.4 percent. For someone weighing the cost of living alone, that spread makes the national average an incomplete guide. The same housing arrangement can come with very different financial demands depending on where you live.

Still, Figure 1 is better read as a comparison than a league table. Its uncertainty bars show that each state’s percentage is an estimate, with some measured less precisely than others. Small gaps between neighboring dots should not become confident claims about which state is more affordable. The chart also leaves out zero- and negative-income households because their rent-to-income ratios cannot be interpreted in the same way. It therefore captures pressure among positive-income renters, rather than the full extent of housing difficulty among everyone renting alone.


Figure 2 gives that pressure a location. Florida, Nevada and several western states stand out. Figure 3, showing where residents live alone, draws attention toward North Dakota and parts of the upper Midwest instead. California sharpens the contrast: just 8.6 percent of its residents lived alone, yet 38.7 percent of its positive-income adult solo renters faced severe burden. Across the 50 states, giving each state equal weight, the correlation between living-alone prevalence and severe burden was approximately −0.49. The pattern is a mismatch worth explaining, not evidence that increasing solo living would make housing cheaper.
Part of the explanation may lie in who appears on each map. A homeowner living alone counts toward Figure 3, but not toward the rental pressure in Figure 2. Figure 3 also covers all ages and compares solo residents with the entire state population. Figure 2 focuses on adult renters with positive income. A high living-alone share therefore does not necessarily mean a high share facing rental costs. Differences in age and homeownership could matter here, although this analysis does not measure their separate effects.
Looking at rent and income together makes the contrast more concrete. Florida’s median annualized gross rent was $19,116, against $10,128 in North Dakota. Median annual income among renters with valid income was $37,000 in Florida and $40,000 in North Dakota. Florida’s higher rent did not come with a higher median income. These medians summarize separate distributions; the burden calculations use each household’s own rent and income, rather than dividing one statewide median by another.
Age adds another twist. Solo renters aged 65 and older paid less at the median: $12,000 in annualized gross rent, compared with $16,200 for those aged 18 to 64. Yet their severe-burden rate was higher, at 41.6 percent versus 29.8 percent. Their median annual income was also much lower: $22,800 versus $43,000. A smaller rent bill can still take a larger bite from a smaller income. That does not mean aging causes housing hardship, and income alone misses savings and assets that some older renters can draw on.
There are limits to the comparison. Gross rent includes utilities and fuel, and annualizes a current monthly amount; income refers to the previous 12 months before taxes. These are existing tenants’ costs, not today’s advertised rents. State-level figures also hide differences between cities and neighborhoods.
The useful next step is to bring the comparison closer to home. Compare apartments within the same local market, including utility costs. Calculate housing costs against dependable income and examine what remains for food, transport and unexpected expenses. If the budget looks tight, consider which adjustment would help most: a different neighborhood, a shared apartment, or a stronger income cushion. The maps provide context for that decision. A place where many people live alone may still demand more of your income than you can comfortably spare.
Data Source: Steven Ruggles, Sarah Flood, Matthew Sobek, Daniel Backman, Grace Cooper, Julia A. Rivera Drew, Stephanie Richards, Renae Rodgers, Jonathan Schroeder, and Kari C.W. Williams. IPUMS USA: Version 16.0 [dataset]. Minneapolis, MN: IPUMS, 2025. https://doi.org/10.18128/D010.V16.0
Here is some additional detailed data; feel free to take a look if you are interested. Also, the analysis code is available in the GitHub Repository.

title: Blog 6: Does One Year of Income Change the Parent–Child Earnings Link?
section: 1. Match Parents and Children with SQL
text:
1. Match Parents and Children with SQL
I use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID): its Parent Identification File links biological parents to children, its individual file tracks people across interviews, and its family files report earnings. Because a family ID can change when someone moves out, a family ID alone cannot identify a person over time. I first link each person’s permanent 1968 family and person identifiers, then use interview-specific family IDs to attach earnings.
After importing and renaming the relevant PSID variables in pandas, I use Python’s sqlite3 to run SQL. This shortened excerpt shows the key matching step:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as db:
    pid.to_sql("pid", db, index=False)
    ind.to_sql("individuals", db, index=False)
    matches = pd.read_sql_query("""
        SELECT p.child_fam68, p.child_pn,
               c.age23 AS child_age23, f.fam99 AS parent_family_1999
        FROM pid AS p
        JOIN individuals AS c
          ON p.child_fam68 = c.fam68 AND p.child_pn = c.pn
        JOIN individuals AS f
          ON p.father_fam68 = f.fam68 AND p.father_pn = f.pn
        JOIN individuals AS m
          ON p.mother_fam68 = m.fam68 AND p.mother_pn = m.pn
        WHERE f.fam99 = m.fam99 AND c.age23 BETWEEN 35 AND 49
    """, db)
SELECT chooses the columns to retain; each JOIN matches records using a two-part person key. The full script also checks parental roles in 1999 and the adult child’s role in 2023, removes invalid IDs, and verifies that each child appears once. These checks matter: an incorrect join could pair the wrong people or duplicate observations.

title: Blog 6: Does One Year of Income Change the Parent–Child Earnings Link?
section: 2. Build Earnings Measures and Estimate IGE
text:
2. Build Earnings Measures and Estimate IGE
Parental earnings combine both biological parents’ labor and business labor earnings; children’s earnings refer to the adult child’s own labor and business labor earnings. The single-year measure uses parental earnings in 1998 and child earnings in 2022 (reported in the 1999 and 2023 interviews). The multi-year measure averages available parental earnings from 1998–2010 and child earnings from 2012–2022, first converting each year’s amount to 2022 dollars using the BLS CPI-U. I require at least three valid parental years and three valid child years for the multi-year estimates.
SQL also makes this aggregation reproducible. After combining both parents’ earnings within each eligible year, the following pattern produces their inflation-adjusted average:
SELECT p.child_fam68, p.child_pn,
       COUNT(*) AS n_parent_years,
       AVG(p.annual_parent_income * 292.655 / c.cpi)
           AS parent_avg_2022usd
FROM parent_income AS p
JOIN cpi AS c ON c.income_year = p.survey_year - 1
GROUP BY p.child_fam68, p.child_pn;
GROUP BY creates one record per child; COUNT counts eligible years and AVG averages real parental earnings. The full pipeline also uses SUM to combine parents’ earnings and repeats the averaging for children. I retain positive values for the two measures used in each regression and estimate:
\[\log(\text{Child earnings})=\alpha+\beta\log(\text{Parent earnings})+\varepsilon.\]
Here, () is the IGE: an estimate of 0.30 means that 10% higher parental earnings are associated with approximately 3% higher adult-child earnings, not that parental earnings cause the increase. Regressions use R’s lm() and 95% confidence intervals with standard errors clustered by parental family to account for siblings.

title: Blog 6: Does One Year of Income Change the Parent–Child Earnings Link?
section: 3. What Changes When We Average Earnings?
text:
3. What Changes When We Average Earnings?
To ensure a fair comparison, both models use the same 1,057 adult children from 728 parental families, aged 35–49 in 2023.

Note: Points show IGE estimates; error bars show 95% confidence intervals clustered by parental family.
The overall single-year IGE is 0.311, compared with 0.372 using multi-year averages. The higher multi-year estimate suggests that one-year earnings can obscure the persistent parent–child relationship through temporary earnings fluctuations.
The age breakdown illustrates why measurement timing deserves attention. For ages 40–44, the multi-year estimate is 0.463, versus 0.302 for a single year. Yet the difference is smaller at ages 35–39 and 45–49, and uncertainty is substantial. Earnings at one age may poorly represent lifetime economic standing—often called life-cycle bias.

title: Blog 6: Does One Year of Income Change the Parent–Child Earnings Link?
text:
Takeaway
In this matched PSID sample, multi-year earnings produce a higher IGE point estimate, consistent with a clearer measure of long-run earnings. The practical lesson is to match people carefully with SQL, average inflation-adjusted earnings when possible, and treat a single year’s IGE as a potentially noisy snapshot—not a complete measure of economic mobility.

Code Reference and Reproducibility
The two code examples above are simplified excerpts from the original analysis scripts. The first example, which demonstrates parent–child matching using SELECT and JOIN in Python’s SQLite environment, is adapted from 03_multiyear_prepare_data.R, lines 175–203. Specifically, lines 175–196 define the SQL matching query, while lines 197–203 show how it is executed through Python’s sqlite3 and pandas. The second example, illustrating GROUP BY, COUNT, and AVG for constructing inflation-adjusted parental earnings, comes from the same file, lines 288–302, particularly the parent_avg operation in lines 294–302. For the single-year parental earnings aggregation using SUM, see 01_singleyear_prepare_data(1).R, lines 182–199. These excerpts omit some data-cleaning steps and sample restrictions for readability. Readers can consult the complete scripts for the full matching procedures, income construction, and reproducible IGE estimates.


Data Availability and Replication
All data used in this analysis are available from the PSID official download page](https://simba.isr.umich.edu/Zips/ZipMain.aspx). Researchers can register for a free account and download the Family Files for every other year from 1999 through 2023 (1999, 2001, …, 2023), along with the Cross-year Individual File (1968–2023) and Parent Identification File (2023).

title: Post 1: Misconceptions About the P-Value
text:
Takeaway
A p-value is not “the probability that the null hypothesis is true.” It is “the probability of observing the current result, or a more extreme one, assuming that the null hypothesis is true.”
The key to understanding the p-value is not memorizing the number (0.05), but remembering the direction of the conditional probability:
\[
P(\text{Data}\mid H_0)
\neq
P(H_0\mid \text{Data})
\]
Once this distinction is clear, the p-value becomes much less mysterious.

title: Blog 7: More Population, More Prosperity?
section: Two Ways an Economy Can Grow
text:
Two Ways an Economy Can Grow
To understand the relationship, we first need to separate two sources of economic growth.
The first is population growth. When a state gains residents, its workforce and consumer base can expand, increasing total economic activity. The second is growth in real GDP per capita, which measures how much inflation-adjusted economic output a state produces per resident.
These two components are connected through a simple relationship:
\[\text{Real GDP} = \text{Population} \times \text{Real GDP per capita}\]
This means that total GDP can increase because the population is growing, because output per person is rising, or because both are happening at the same time.
In terms of annual growth rates, the exact relationship is:
\[g_{GDP}=g_{POP}+g_{PC}+g_{POP}g_{PC}\]
The final term accounts for the interaction between population growth and per-capita GDP growth. Because this term is usually small, the two growth rates can be added together to provide a close approximation of total GDP growth.
This distinction matters because the two sources of growth tell us different things. Population growth describes an increase in economic scale, while growth in real GDP per capita provides a measure of whether economic output is increasing relative to the number of people who live in the state.
To see how these forces have evolved, I use annual data for all 50 states between 2000 and 2025, with annual growth rates calculated from 2001 onward.






Figure 1. Decomposition of annual real GDP growth across 50 states, 2001–2025. Choose a year with the slider; hover to read a state’s three rates. The bars show approximate additive contributions; the dot is the actual GDP change. For the clearest view of all 50 states, use a desktop-width browser window.

title: Blog 7: More Population, More Prosperity?
section: What Happens When We Follow States Over Time?
text:
What Happens When We Follow States Over Time?
Rather than comparing states at just one point in time, the chart allows us to follow the same states through economic expansions, recessions, and recoveries. This makes it easier to see why population growth and overall economic performance do not always move together.
Consider 2009, when the Great Recession was affecting economies across the country. In that year, 39 states experienced population growth even as their total real GDP declined. These states were gaining residents, but the decline in economic output per person was large enough to outweigh the contribution of population growth.
A similar pattern appeared in 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted economic activity. In 37 states, population increased while total real GDP fell. Once again, having more residents did not prevent the overall economy from contracting.
The following year tells a very different story. In 2021, real GDP per capita increased in all 50 states as economic activity rebounded. The improvement was broad-based, rather than limited to states experiencing rapid population growth.
Taken together, these years illustrate why population growth alone cannot explain a state’s economic performance. Population may continue to rise through a downturn, but whether total output expands or contracts depends heavily on what happens to output per resident.

title: Blog 7: More Population, More Prosperity?
section: More People, More GDP—but Not Necessarily More GDP per Person
text:
More People, More GDP—but Not Necessarily More GDP per Person
Across the 50 states, annualized population growth between 2000 and 2025 has a positive correlation of 0.77 with annualized total real GDP growth. States that gained population more rapidly generally also experienced faster growth in the overall size of their economies. However, the correlation between population growth and real GDP-per-capita growth is 0.08, indicating almost no linear relationship across states over this period.
There is a straightforward reason for this contrast. More residents can contribute to a larger total economy even when output per resident changes very little. But adding people does not, by itself, ensure that economic output grows faster than the population.
The experiences of Nevada and Utah make this difference especially clear.
Between 2000 and 2025, Nevada’s population grew at an annualized rate of approximately 1.96%, among the faster rates in the country. Yet its real GDP per capita grew by only 0.47% per year. The state’s economy expanded substantially in size, but growth in output per resident was relatively modest.
Utah experienced similarly rapid population growth, averaging 1.84% per year. Unlike Nevada, however, Utah also recorded strong real GDP-per-capita growth of 1.80% annually.
Both states became significantly more populous, but their economic trajectories differed. Utah combined population expansion with much faster growth in output per resident, while Nevada’s overall economic expansion relied more heavily on the addition of people.
The comparison shows why population growth should not be treated as a substitute for per-capita economic performance. Two states can attract residents at similar rates while experiencing very different outcomes in how much output they produce per person.
The most recent year in the dataset offers another useful comparison. In 2025, Texas experienced population growth of approximately 1.25%, alongside real GDP growth of 2.85%. California, by contrast, had a nearly unchanged population, with a slight decline of 0.02%, yet its real GDP grew by 3.54%.
California’s economy therefore grew faster than Texas’s that year despite having virtually no population growth. The difference reflects stronger growth in output per resident, illustrating that a state does not need rapid population expansion to achieve substantial overall economic growth.
You can explore this contrast directly in Figure 1 by moving the slider to 2025 and hovering over Texas and California.

title: Blog 7: More Population, More Prosperity?
text:
What Can We Actually Conclude?
Population growth can make a state’s economy growth. What it cannot guarantee is that the economy will generate more output for each person who lives there.
That is the central lesson of the past 25 years. During recessions, many states continued gaining residents while their economies contracted. During recoveries, per-capita output rose broadly, including in states without exceptionally strong population growth. And over the full period, states with similar population trends often followed very different paths in real GDP per capita.
For policymakers, the implication is not that attracting residents is unimportant. Rather, population growth should be understood as one part of a broader economic strategy, not as the ultimate measure of its success.
A larger population creates opportunities, but turning those opportunities into lasting economic progress depends on factors such as productive investment, workers’ skills, infrastructure, and the ability of businesses to generate greater value.
The goal, ultimately, should not be simply to build a bigger economy. It should be to build an economy that produces more for the people who live in it.


Data and Methodology
I collected annual population and real GDP data for all 50 U.S. states from 2000 to 2025 using the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) API. Population data originate from the U.S. Census Bureau, while real GDP data come from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), measured in inflation-adjusted chained 2017 dollars. Using R, we downloaded the datasets, checked their completeness, and verified that each state had observations for all 26 years. We then calculated annual population growth, real GDP growth, and real GDP per capita growth to distinguish economic expansion associated with population increases from growth in output per resident. We also calculated the ratio of population growth to real GDP growth to examine how their relative magnitudes varied across states and years. Finally, we used Plotly in R to create two interactive visualizations, allowing readers to compare population and real GDP across states and explore changes in population’s share of GDP growth over time through year sliders and hover information. These comparisons are descriptive and do not establish a causal effect of population growth on GDP.
For the specific code and data to reproduce the results, please visit RodgersYe_6400_Blog07

title: Post 2: What Is the Best Day of the Week for Attending Drexel Events?
section: When Should You Keep Your Schedule Open?
text:
When Should You Keep Your Schedule Open?
University event calendars can be overwhelming. Talks, workshops, exhibitions, career events, and student activities are spread across the week, but they are not necessarily distributed evenly. If someone wants to attend more campus events, does it matter which days they keep relatively flexible?
To answer this question, I analyzed events listed on the Drexel University Events Calendar for 2026. My research question is:
Which day or days of the week offer the most opportunities among events currently listed on the Drexel University Events Calendar for 2026?
The goal is not simply to count events. I want to turn publicly available calendar data into a practical scheduling recommendation.

title: Post 2: What Is the Best Day of the Week for Attending Drexel Events?
text:
Scraping and Cleaning the Calendar
I collected the data from the Drexel University Events Calendar using R and the rvest package. Before scraping, I checked the site’s robots rules and confirmed that the calendar page was not disallowed. To limit the burden on the website, I requested only one monthly calendar page at a time and added a two-second pause between requests.
The scraping script collected event titles, dates, event IDs, and URLs for January through December 2026. It produced 3,869 raw calendar records.
The raw data required cleaning. Events explicitly marked as cancelled were removed. This eliminated 292 calendar records representing four unique cancelled events. I also checked for exact duplicates based on event ID, information ID, and date, but found none.


# A tibble: 7 × 6
   rank weekday   number_of_events number_of_calendar_days events_per_weekday
  <dbl> <chr>                <dbl>                   <dbl>              <dbl>
1     1 Tuesday                707                      52              13.6 
2     2 Wednesday              701                      52              13.5 
3     3 Thursday               658                      53              12.4 
4     4 Monday                 466                      52               8.96
5     5 Friday                 459                      52               8.83
6     6 Saturday               331                      52               6.37
7     7 Sunday                 255                      52               4.9 
# ℹ 1 more variable: share_percent <dbl>


One important choice was how to handle multi-day and recurring events. I treated an event appearing on multiple dates as multiple attendance opportunities because a person could potentially attend it on different days. However, I also performed a robustness check excluding events explicitly labeled as multi-day events.

title: Post 2: What Is the Best Day of the Week for Attending Drexel Events?
text:
Tuesdays and Wednesdays Stand Out
The cleaned dataset contains 3,577 event occurrences. Tuesdays had 707 listed opportunities and Wednesdays had 701. Because weekdays do not all occur exactly the same number of times in a calendar year, I divided the number of events by the number of occurrences of each weekday in 2026.









A typical Tuesday had about 13.6 listed event opportunities, compared with 13.5 on Wednesday and 12.4 on Thursday. The numbers fall substantially toward the weekend: Saturday averaged about 6.4 and Sunday only 4.9.
The difference between Tuesday and Wednesday is extremely small, so it would be misleading to claim that Tuesday is decisively the single best day.

title: Post 2: What Is the Best Day of the Week for Attending Drexel Events?
text:
Does the Result Hold Up?
There are two important concerns. First, the data were scraped on September 21, 2026, so events later in the year may not yet be fully posted. Second, long-running events could disproportionately affect weekday counts.
I therefore repeated the analysis using only events occurring on or before September 21. In that sample, Wednesday ranked slightly above Tuesday. I also excluded events explicitly labeled as multi-day events; in that version, Tuesday ranked first and Wednesday second.
Across all three specifications, the broader pattern remained the same: Tuesday and Wednesday consistently had the highest concentration of event opportunities, with Thursday close behind.

title: Post 2: What Is the Best Day of the Week for Attending Drexel Events?
text:
Takeaway
For someone trying to maximize opportunities to attend events listed on Drexel’s calendar, the most useful scheduling strategy is not to focus on one single “best” day. Instead, keeping Tuesdays and Wednesdays relatively flexible provides the greatest access to events, while Thursdays are another strong option.
The analysis also illustrates an important lesson from web scraping: collecting the data is only the first step. Cleaning repeated listings, defining what counts as an opportunity, and recognizing incomplete future schedules are necessary before scraped data can support a useful real-world decision.

title: Blog 4: The Price Tag Behind America’s Income Rankings
text:
In 2024, California ranked fourth among the 50 states in nominal per capita personal income; South Dakota ranked 13th. After adjusting income for local prices, South Dakota rose to fourth and California fell to 12th. No one’s income changed because of this calculation. What changed was the yardstick used to compare it.
That reversal caught my attention because of a familiar problem in a job search. If two hypothetical jobs each offered $80,000, they would look tied in the salary column. Once I considered rent, groceries, and transportation in each location, the comparison would become less straightforward. A state’s average income cannot tell me what either job would pay, and a state’s average price level is not my personal budget. Still, the example raises a broader question: when we call a state “high income,” do we also assume that money goes further there? Would the highest-income states still lead after accounting for local prices?
To examine that question, I compare the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s (BEA) per capita personal income across the 50 states in 2024. The measure includes income beyond wages. For prices, I use BEA’s regional price parities(RPPs) for the same year. With the national price level set to 100, an RPP describes a state’s relative prices for goods and services; housing is only one component. I divide each state’s nominal per capita income by its RPP divided by 100. An RPP of 110 means dividing income by 1.10; an RPP of 90 means dividing it by 0.90. The result compares state incomes on a common price basis. It is not a measure of anyone’s paycheck.
Both maps use the same color scale: darker states rank higher, though the colors do not show how many dollars separate them. On the nominal map, dark colors appear in the Northeast and California, but also in Wyoming. Wyoming already ranked third, so the original list was never a simple contest between the coasts and the interior. On the adjusted map, the middle of the country becomes more prominent. Wyoming moves to first, while South Dakota, Nebraska, and North Dakota enter the top ten. South Dakota stands out because it began outside that group.


The other half of the maps matters just as much. California slips from fourth to 12th, and Hawaii becomes much lighter. Yet Connecticut and Massachusetts remain second and third. Local prices change some important positions without pushing high-income states as a group out of the lead. Telling only South Dakota’s rise or California’s fall would miss that tension.
The top ten provide a useful check: seven of the original ten states remain there after the adjustment. Across all 50 states, 44 change rank, but the median absolute change is just four places. “Many states moved” does not mean “the whole ranking was overturned.” For a few states, prices substantially change the impression given by nominal income. For most, the shift is smaller.
How uneven are those moves? The third figure puts every state on the same rank-change scale. Zero means no change; blue marks a move toward first place, and orange a move away from it. Iowa and Oklahoma each climb 17 places, and Louisiana climbs 13. At the other end, Hawaii falls 26 places, Oregon 15, and Florida 13. Six states do not move at all. Hawaii’s long line draws the eye, but it does not represent the many shorter lines around it.

There is another trap in reading this figure: a change in rank is not the size of an income difference. Iowa climbs 17 places but still ranks 18th; the chart cannot tell us how many dollars separate it from the state above it. Delaware shows why rankings are relative in another way. Its overall price level is slightly below the national average, yet it falls ten places. There is no contradiction. When all 50 states are reordered together, other states can gain more ground and push Delaware down. A falling rank does not, by itself, mean a state’s prices are above the national average.
These figures also have clear limits. Per capita personal income is an average, not the income of a typical resident or a job offer; it includes sources beyond wages. RPP describes prices across an entire state, not the particular city where I might live, whether I rent or own, or what I buy. Taxes, school and healthcare quality, commuting, and other aspects of daily life are outside this calculation. Finally, these are two rankings of the same year, not a record of how residents’ purchasing power changed over time. They cannot establish why a state moved.
The two hypothetical $80,000 jobs still have no winner that I can read from a map. This analysis answers a narrower question: what do we miss when we look only at a list of high-income states? Nominal income is a useful starting point, but it leaves out local prices. For most states, turning over that price tag moves the ranking only a few places. For a handful, it changes who belongs in the top ten.
